chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from al-Nadr ibn Shu'ayb, from Abdul Ghaffar al-Jazzi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a man who died while he had a debt upon him. He said: If wealth came into his hands without corruption, Allah will not hold him accountable when He knows of his intention [to pay], except for the one who did not intend to pay from his trust, so he is like the thief; and similarly is the Zakat, and similarly is the one who permits himself to take away the dowries of the women.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a deceased person's unpaid debts if they intended to pay them?
ai.summary: In al-Kafi, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that a deceased debtor is exempt from accountability if the debt arose from lawful transactions and he possessed the sincere intention to repay, distinguishing this from intentional defaulters who are likened to thieves. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on internal intent (niyyah) alongside external obligation, extending the principle to Zakat and dowries to highlight the sanctity of fulfilling trusts. The hadith serves as a critical link between personal piety and social justice, ensuring that financial obligations are viewed as sacred trusts rather than mere legal liabilities.
